title: Uncork a wine bottle in its cradle
instruction: Open the bottle of wine without taking it out of its cradle, and leave the cork off it.
context: Opening a bottle of wine is one of the most familiar jobs at home and at the table. A natural cork grips the neck so hard (about 200 N to draw it, as measured in published tests) that it is pulled with a lever corkscrew; an older red is opened lying in its pouring cradle so that its sediment stays settled.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A fixed beech pouring cradle on the table: two slats under the bottle's body on two posts, a back board behind the bottle's base and a base board. (2) A full 75 cl Bordeaux bottle of red wine in the cradle, dark green glass, 1.25 kg (0.5 kg of glass): a body 75 mm across and 190 mm long, a shoulder, and a neck 29 mm across with a 31 mm bead at the mouth and a 17.7 mm bore (the bore of the bottles in the published measurement in (3)); its foil capsule is cut away below the bead. It lies tipped up 10 degrees, its neck pointing back toward the right arm, 55 degrees from the left-right line; the middle of its mouth is 32 cm forward, 2 cm right of the centre line and 10.1 cm above the table. (3) A one-piece natural cork, 38 x 24 mm (3.5 g), compressed into the bore with its outer face flush with the lip; it takes 196 N to start it. That figure is a published measurement, not ours: Giunchi, Versari, Parpinello and Galassi (2008), Journal of Food Engineering 88(4), 576-580, doi:10.1016/j.jfoodeng.2008.03.004, measured 196 ± 20 N (mean ± SD) for a natural cork pulled from a 750 ml bottle with a 17.7 mm neck, 24 h after bottling, as in ISO 9727-5, on a texture analyser with a 4 mm corkscrew and a 500 N load cell at 5 mm/s. We could not find the cork's size or surface treatment in the paper, so the 38 mm length is our choice (a standard length for 75 cl bottles, short enough for the corkscrew's 45 mm stroke to draw it fully). (4) A chrome-plated zinc wing corkscrew, 167 mm long and 250 g, set on the mouth with its wings down: a bell 39 mm across, whose collar fits over the bead and whose inner ring sits on the lip, with windows in its top and bottom; a steel rack (12 mm, ring teeth) sliding in the bell; a steel worm (5 turns, 50 mm, 10 mm pitch) on a spindle that turns in the rack, its point resting on the middle of the cork, and a square knob (16 mm across its flats, 14 mm long) on top; and two wings, each a lever 112.5 mm from its pivot to a round paddle (24 mm across, 16 mm deep), with a pinion (17.5 mm pitch radius) meshing with the rack. Turning the knob clockwise screws the worm into the cork, which draws the rack in and raises the wings; pressing the wings back down draws the rack and the cork out, with 6.4 times the push at the paddles. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot. Batch check before any real trials (the measurement for the cork batch in use): fill five bottles of the trial type (17.7 mm bore), cork them flush with new corks from the batch with a four-jaw hand or bench corker, wait 24 h, then pull each cork with a corkscrew on a motorised test stand with a digital force gauge at 300 mm/min (5 mm/s) and record the peak force, as in ISO 9727-5. Accept the batch if the mean of the five lies within the source's 196 ± 20 N (176 to 216 N); otherwise set the simulated grip to the batch's mean and re-run the demonstration. Reset between trials: take the corkscrew off, lay another full bottle of the same type in the cradle at its marks, corked flush with a new cork from the accepted batch at least 24 h before (as in the measurement), and set the corkscrew on its mouth with its wings down and its point on the middle of the cork.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. Out: the cork's inner end has passed the lip (measured: the cork is free of the neck, judged from the video). Off: the cork's middle at least 6 cm from the middle of the mouth (measured with a ruler, or the cork away from the mouth in the video). In its cradle: the bottle moved no more than 2 cm and its axis turned no more than 5 degrees (measured against tape marks on the cradle). 1.0: the cork out and off with the bottle in its cradle; 0.5: the cork drawn at least 10 mm out of the neck (measured: how far the cork stands proud of the lip); 0.25: the worm turned at least 20 mm into the cork, two turns past where it caught (measured: count the turns of the knob, or the rack's travel); else 0.0. 0.0 for good once the bottle has been taken out of its cradle (moved more than 5 cm or its axis turned more than 15 degrees at any time). The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the bottle, the cork and the corkscrew still and both hands still and at least 10 cm clear of them.
reset_notes: Take the corkscrew off and unscrew the cork from its worm; lay another full bottle of the same type (17.7 mm bore) in the cradle at its marks, corked flush with a new natural cork from the accepted batch at least 24 h before with a hand or bench corker; set the corkscrew on its mouth, wings down, its point on the middle of the cork. Before any trials, accept the cork batch with the five-bottle extraction check in the setup (mean within 176-216 N).
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Stand-ins: the cork's fit is a slide whose drive is capped at its friction (196 N, a published measured mean for a natural cork in this bore, not our measurement; falling with the length left in the neck); the thread is a slide following the turns; the rack and pinions mesh through stiff drives re-aimed every physics step; the bell's collar is a joint. The cork weighs 10 g (real 3.5 g) for solver stability. Cameras 1280 x 704.
